title: Whale Sharks of the Red Sea
summary: How the whale shark, the largest fish on Earth, breathes, filter-feeds, is identified by its spots, gathers near Al-Lith in the Red Sea, and can be protected.
poll: People should be allowed to swim close to wild whale sharks.

versions.title: The Big Spotted Fish
versions.text:
A huge fish swims in the Red Sea. It is a whale shark. It is the biggest fish in the world. It is as long as a bus!

It is not a whale. It is a shark. It has gills. The gills take air from the water.

This shark does not hunt big fish. It eats tiny things. They are plankton. The shark swims with its mouth wide. Water goes in. Pads by the gills filter the food out. Then the water goes out.

The shark is calm. It swims slow. It will not hurt you.

Its back has white spots. No two sharks have the same spots. So we take a photo of the spots. Then we know which shark it is.

In spring, lots of young sharks come to a reef. It is near Al-Lith in Saudi Arabia. Some get tags.

Whale sharks are endangered. Boats can hit them. Nets can trap them. Trash can hurt them. Do not touch them. Stay back. Just watch.

versions.title: The Big Spotted Fish
versions.text:
A huge fish swims in the Red Sea. It is called a whale shark. It is the biggest fish in the world. It can be as long as a school bus!

The whale shark is not a whale. It is a shark. Like all fish, it has gills. It gets the air it needs from the water with its gills.

This shark does not hunt big fish. It eats tiny plants and animals. They are called plankton. The shark swims with its mouth open wide. Water rushes in. Pads near the gills filter out the food. Then the water flows back out.

The whale shark is calm. It swims slowly. It does not hurt people.

Its dark back is full of white spots. No two sharks have the same spots. So people take photos of the spots. That is how they can tell which shark is which.

Each spring, lots of young whale sharks come to a reef. It is near the town of Al-Lith in Saudi Arabia. People there put tags on some sharks to learn where they go.

Whale sharks are endangered. Boats can hit them. Fishing nets can trap them. Trash in the sea can hurt them. If you see one, do not touch it. Stay back and watch.

versions.title: Whale Sharks: Gentle Giants
versions.text:
A giant fish glides through the warm blue water of the Red Sea. It is a whale shark, the biggest fish in the world. It can grow as long as a school bus!

Even with its name, the whale shark is not a whale. Whales must swim up to breathe air. A whale shark is a fish, so it uses gills. Its gills take in the air that is in the water.

This huge shark does not hunt big animals. It eats tiny living things called plankton. To feed, the shark swims with its wide mouth open. Water rushes in. Special pads near its gills filter out the food. Then the water flows back out through the gills.

Whale sharks are calm and slow. They do not harm people.

Each shark has a dark back covered with white spots. No two sharks have the same pattern. Scientists take photos of the spots to tell one shark from another.

Every spring, many young whale sharks gather at a reef near the town of Al-Lith in Saudi Arabia. Scientists put tags on some of them to learn where they travel.

Sadly, whale sharks are endangered. Boats can hit them, nets can trap them, and trash can hurt them. If you ever see one, do not touch it. Give it space and enjoy watching.

versions.title: Whale Sharks: Gentle Giants
versions.text:
A giant fish glides slowly through the warm blue water of the Red Sea. It is a whale shark, the largest fish on Earth. An adult can grow about twelve meters long. That is as long as a school bus.

Despite its name, the whale shark is not a whale. Whales are mammals. They must swim up to the surface to breathe air. A whale shark is a fish, and it breathes with gills. Its gills take oxygen from the water.

This enormous shark does not hunt large animals. Instead, it eats plankton, which are tiny plants and animals that drift in the sea. To feed, the shark swims with its huge mouth wide open. Water pours in. Special pads near its gills filter out the food. Then the water flows back out through the gills.

Whale sharks are calm, slow swimmers, and they are not dangerous to people.

Every whale shark has a dark back covered with white spots and stripes. No two sharks have the same pattern, just as no two people have the same fingerprints. Scientists photograph the spots to identify each shark.

Each spring, many young whale sharks gather at a reef near the town of Al-Lith, on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia. Scientists attach tags to some of them to learn where they travel.

Sadly, whale sharks are endangered. Boats can strike them, fishing nets can trap them, and plastic trash can harm them. If you ever meet one, do not touch it. Give it plenty of space.

versions.title: Whale Sharks of the Red Sea
versions.text:
A giant shadow moves slowly beneath the surface of the Red Sea. Divers hold their breath as it comes closer. It is a whale shark, the largest fish on Earth. An adult can grow about twelve meters long and weigh as much as two or three elephants.

Despite its name, the whale shark is not a whale. Whales are mammals that must come up to breathe air. The whale shark is a fish, and it breathes with gills that take oxygen from the water.

The whale shark is a filter feeder. It eats plankton, which are tiny plants and animals that drift in the water, along with fish eggs and small fish. It swims with its huge mouth wide open, and as water rushes in, spongy pads near the gills trap the food. The water then flows out through the gills. Although the shark has thousands of tiny teeth, it does not use them to eat.

Whale sharks are gentle and slow, so they are not a danger to people.

Each shark has a dark back covered with white spots and pale stripes. No two sharks share the same pattern, so scientists use photos of the spots to identify each one.

Every spring, many young whale sharks gather at a reef near Al-Lith, a town on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia. Scientists attach small tags to some sharks, and the tags show that whale sharks migrate long distances to find food.

Today, whale sharks are endangered. Boats strike them, fishing nets trap them, and plastic pollutes their waters. People who snorkel near them should never touch them and should always keep a safe distance.

versions.title: Giants of the Red Sea
versions.text:

The divers floating nearby hold their breath as it approaches, because they recognize the outline of a whale shark, the largest fish on Earth. A fully grown adult can reach approximately twelve meters in length and may weigh as much as two or three elephants combined.

The whale shark is a filter feeder that consumes plankton, the microscopic plants and animals drifting through the ocean, together with fish eggs and small fish. Sometimes it cruises forward with its enormous mouth open, and at other times it hangs almost upright and gulps water like a powerful vacuum. Spongy filter pads near the gills capture the food while the water escapes through the gill openings. Although the shark possesses thousands of tiny teeth, it does not use them for eating.

Whale sharks are gentle, slow-moving creatures that present no danger to people.

Conservation experts believe that sustainable tourism can help, provided that snorkelers never touch the sharks and always maintain a respectful distance.

Despite its misleading name, the whale shark is not a whale. Whales are mammals that must periodically rise to the surface in order to breathe atmospheric air, whereas the whale shark is a fish that respires through gills, which extract dissolved oxygen directly from the surrounding seawater.

Most of these seasonal visitors are juvenile sharks measuring only about four meters in length, considerably smaller than fully mature adults. versions.title: Whale Sharks of the Red Sea
versions.text:
A gigantic shadow glides deliberately beneath the surface of the Red Sea, and the divers floating nearby hold their breath involuntarily as it approaches, because they immediately recognize the unmistakable silhouette of a whale shark, the largest fish species found anywhere on this planet. A fully grown adult can reach approximately twelve meters in length and may weigh as much as two or three elephants combined, an almost incomprehensible biological mass for a creature that nonetheless drifts so gracefully through open water with apparent effortlessness.

Despite its somewhat misleading common name, the whale shark is not, in any taxonomic sense, a whale at all. Whales are mammals that must periodically rise to the surface in order to breathe atmospheric air directly, whereas the whale shark is unambiguously a fish that respires continuously through gills, specialized structures that extract dissolved oxygen directly from the surrounding seawater without ever requiring a trip to the surface for that specific purpose.

The whale shark functions as an obligate filter feeder that consumes plankton, the countless microscopic organisms drifting throughout the open ocean, together with fish eggs and assorted small fish. Occasionally it cruises steadily forward through the water with its enormous mouth held wide open, while at other times it positions its entire massive body almost vertically and gulps the surrounding water like an immensely powerful biological vacuum. Spongy filter pads located near the gills capture the available nourishment with considerable efficiency while the water itself escapes harmlessly through the gill openings. Although the shark possesses thousands of tiny, functionally vestigial teeth, it does not use them for feeding purposes at all, a trait that distinguishes it fundamentally from its considerably more predatory relatives among the broader shark family.

These gentle, unhurried creatures present absolutely no danger to human beings under ordinary circumstances, and females give birth to fully live young rather than depositing eggs upon the seafloor as many other fish species do, a reproductive strategy that remains incompletely understood even by professional marine biologists who have devoted entire careers to studying the species.

Every whale shark displays a dark back decorated with distinctive white spots and pale stripes arranged in an entirely unique pattern specific to that individual. Because no two individuals ever display precisely the same arrangement of markings, researchers compare photographs of these distinctive spots to identify particular sharks across many successive years of observation, a technique broadly comparable to the identification of human fingerprints by forensic investigators working a case.

Every spring, a substantial aggregation of whale sharks reliably assembles at a coral reef near Al-Lith, situated along the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia. Most of these seasonal visitors are juvenile sharks measuring only about four meters in length, considerably smaller than the fully mature adults found elsewhere. Scientists affiliated with Saudi universities have attached satellite tags to several of these juveniles, generating valuable longitudinal data which demonstrates conclusively that these young sharks travel extensively across the entire Red Sea basin and occasionally venture considerably beyond its geographic boundaries.

Whale sharks are now officially classified as endangered, because their global population has declined dramatically and alarmingly during recent decades across virtually every ocean basin they historically inhabited. Boats collide with them, fishing nets entangle them, and plastic pollution continues steadily accumulating throughout their shared marine habitat. Conservation specialists therefore argue persuasively that carefully regulated, genuinely sustainable ecotourism can benefit both coastal communities and the sharks themselves in tandem, provided that participating snorkelers never touch the animals and consistently maintain a respectful distance from them at all times during every encounter.

questions.stem: The article calls the whale shark a filter feeder. Which detail best explains this term?
options: It has thousands of tiny teeth.
It swims slowly near divers.
Pads near its gills trap food as water flows out.
It has white spots and pale stripes.
questions.why: A filter feeder strains food from water. The pads near the gills trap the food while the water leaves.

wrong.A: The article says it does not use its teeth to eat.
wrong.B: Swimming slowly does not explain how it feeds.
wrong.D: The spots help identify sharks, not feed them.

questions.stem: Why do scientists compare photographs of the spots instead of measuring each shark?
options: Measuring a shark is against the law.
Each shark has its own pattern of spots.
The spots change color every year.
Photos show how much plankton the shark ate.
questions.why: No two sharks share the same pattern, like fingerprints, so a photo is an easy way to recognize one shark again.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about laws on measuring.
wrong.C: The article does not say the spots change.
wrong.D: Photos of spots do not show what the shark ate.

questions.stem: Why does the article say snorkelers should keep a safe distance?
options: Because the sharks bite people who come close
Because the water near the sharks is too cold
Because snorkelers scare away the plankton
Because the sharks are endangered and need to be protected
questions.why: The rule comes right after the article explains that whale sharks are endangered, so keeping away helps protect them.

wrong.A: The article says whale sharks are not a danger to people.
wrong.C: The article does not say snorkelers scare plankton.

questions.stem: How is a whale shark different from a whale?
options: A whale shark breathes with gills, but a whale must come up for air.
A whale shark is a mammal, but a whale is a fish.
A whale shark rests on land, but a whale lives in the deep sea.
A whale shark has no spots, but a whale does.
questions.why: The article says whales are mammals that come up to breathe, while the whale shark is a fish with gills.

wrong.B: This is backward: whales are mammals and the whale shark is a fish.
wrong.D: The whale shark is the one with spots.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: As a story told by a diver from beginning to end
As a list of steps for catching a shark
As sections that each describe one part of the whale shark's life and protection
As a comparison of every kind of shark
questions.why: After the opening scene, each paragraph covers one topic: size, breathing, feeding, spots, the Al-Lith reef, and threats.

wrong.A: Only the opening describes divers; the rest gives facts.
wrong.B: The article does not give steps for catching sharks.
wrong.D: Other sharks are not compared.

MID.prompt: Explain how a whale shark eats, using the term filter feeder. Then explain one reason whale sharks are endangered.
checklist: I explained how the pads near the gills trap food.
I gave one danger to whale sharks from the article.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: A whale shark is a filter feeder, which means it swims with its enormous mouth open and spongy filter pads near its gills trap plankton, fish eggs, and small fish as the water flows back out. One reason whale sharks are endangered is that fishing nets can trap them, since the article explains that boats, nets, and plastic pollution all put these gentle giants at risk.

keyWords.definition: a large group of animals gathered in one place at the same time
keyWords.example: An aggregation of flamingos turned the lake pink.

keyWords.definition: young and not yet fully grown
keyWords.example: The juvenile falcon was still learning how to hunt.

keyWords.definition: a machine in space that circles the Earth and sends information back
keyWords.example: A weather satellite helps forecasters see storms coming.

keyWords.definition: the protection of animals, plants, and natural places
keyWords.example: Conservation groups planted mangrove trees along the coast.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without harming nature
keyWords.example: Using reusable bags is a sustainable habit.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Whale sharks are mysterious, so scientists have stopped studying them.
Ecotourism is the main reason whale sharks are endangered.
This gentle giant needs research and careful protection to survive.
Whale sharks in the Red Sea are all fully grown adults.
questions.why: The article describes the shark's biology, the research at Al-Lith, and the threats and conservation ideas that could protect it.

wrong.A: The article describes active research with photos and satellite tags.
wrong.B: The article presents careful ecotourism as a possible help, not the cause.
wrong.D: The article says most sharks at Al-Lith are juveniles.

questions.stem: According to the article, what are the whale sharks near Al-Lith mostly like?
options: Juveniles about four meters long
Adults about twenty meters long
Females waiting to lay eggs
Sharks that never leave the reef
questions.why: The article says most of the visitors are juvenile sharks measuring only about four meters long.

wrong.B: They are young, not adults, and the article gives four meters.
wrong.C: Whale sharks give birth to live young; they do not lay eggs.
wrong.D: The satellite tags show they travel widely.

questions.stem: What does the article say about how whale sharks have their young?
options: They lay eggs on the seafloor.
They build nests in coral reefs.
Females give birth to live young.
They hatch their eggs in their mouths.
questions.why: The article states that females give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.

wrong.A: The article says this is exactly what they do NOT do.
wrong.D: This idea does not appear in the article.

questions.stem: The writer says the shark 'gulps water like a powerful vacuum.' What does this comparison suggest?
options: The shark makes a loud noise when it eats.
The shark pulls in water and food with great force.
The shark cleans the seafloor of trash.
The shark swallows divers by accident.
questions.why: A vacuum sucks things in strongly, so the comparison shows the shark drawing in water and food forcefully.

wrong.A: The comparison is about suction, not sound.
wrong.C: The shark eats plankton; it does not clean up trash.
wrong.D: The article says whale sharks present no danger to people.

questions.stem: Why might satellite tags be more useful than photographs for studying these sharks?
options: Tags change the color of the shark's spots.
Photos cannot show which shark is which.
Tags can follow where a shark travels after it leaves the reef.
Photos can only be taken at night.
questions.why: Photos identify a shark when people see it, but tags send data as the shark travels across and beyond the Red Sea.

wrong.B: The article says photos of spots do identify individual sharks.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests photos are limited to night.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer from the fact that the reef near Al-Lith attracts the sharks every spring?
options: The sharks are lost and cannot find the open sea.
The reef is the only place whale sharks can breathe.
Saudi universities feed the sharks each spring.
Protecting the reef could help the sharks.
questions.why: Since the sharks return every spring, the reef matters to them, and protecting it supports their survival.

wrong.A: The tags show they travel widely, so they are not lost.
wrong.B: Sharks breathe with gills everywhere in the sea.
wrong.C: The article says universities tag the sharks, not feed them.

questions.stem: According to the article, why could sustainable ecotourism help whale sharks?
options: It rewards communities that protect the sharks, if visitors follow rules.
It teaches the sharks to trust the boats that bring tourists.
It removes all plastic from the Red Sea.
It lets snorkelers touch and feed the sharks whenever they like.
questions.why: The article says regulated ecotourism can benefit communities and sharks if snorkelers never touch them and keep their distance.

wrong.B: Boats are a danger; the article does not say sharks should trust them.
wrong.C: The article does not claim ecotourism removes all plastic.
wrong.D: The article says snorkelers should never touch the animals.

questions.stem: Why does the author open the article with divers watching a shadow approach?
options: To prove that diving is dangerous
To create curiosity before revealing the whale shark
To explain how divers breathe underwater
To compare the Red Sea with other oceans
questions.why: The mysterious shadow builds suspense and draws readers in before the author names the whale shark.

wrong.A: The article says the shark is no danger to people.
wrong.D: No other oceans are compared.

HIGH.prompt: Using evidence from the article, explain how scientists study whale sharks in the Red Sea and how that research could support their conservation.
checklist: I described both photo identification and satellite tags.
I connected the research to protecting the sharks.
I used at least two key words such as aggregation, juvenile, or sustainable.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Scientists study whale sharks in the Red Sea in two main ways. First, because every shark's pattern of spots and stripes is unique, researchers compare photographs to identify individual sharks during the spring aggregation of young whale sharks near Al-Lith. Second, researchers attach small electronic tags that reveal how these juvenile sharks migrate long distances in search of food. This research directly supports conservation, because understanding where and when whale sharks gather and travel helps people create more sustainable fishing and boating rules that protect the sharks from being struck or trapped.
